title: The Relative Sentence (Jumlat al-Ṣilah)
source: Original instructional lesson authored for this application (syllabus ref: Haywood & Nahmad Ch. 34; Ryding Ch. 14)
objectives: Select the correct relative pronoun (الَّذِي, الَّتِي, الَّذِينَ, اللَّاتِي) for definite antecedents.
Form asyndetic relative clauses (omitting the relative pronoun) after indefinite antecedents.
Identify the returning resumptive pronoun (al-ʿāʾid) linking the relative clause back to the antecedent.
recallPrompt: From Chapter 11: Why must an attributive modifier match its noun in definiteness?

sections.heading: Definite vs. Indefinite Relative Clauses
sections.body: Arabic relative clauses follow a strict definiteness rule: if the antecedent noun is DEFINITE, you must use a relative pronoun (al-ism al-mawṣūl: الَّذِي, الَّتِي, etc.). If the antecedent is INDEFINITE, you MUST omit the relative pronoun completely—the modifying clause follows directly.

sections.label: The Returning Pronoun (Al-ʿĀʾid)
sections.summary: When the antecedent functions as the direct object or object of a preposition inside the relative clause, Arabic inserts a resumptive pronoun (al-ʿāʾid) agreeing with the antecedent (e.g., الكِتَابُ الَّذِي قَرَأْتُهُ 'the book which I read [it]').

sections.arabic: هٰذَا هُوَ البَيْتُ الَّذِي سَكَنْتُ فِيهِ
sections.transliteration: hādhā huwa l-baytu lladhī sakantu fīhi
sections.translation: This is the house in which I lived.
sections.irab: البَيْتُ: خَبَرٌ مَرْفُوعٌ | الَّذِي: اسْمٌ مَوْصُولٌ نَعْتٌ | سَكَنْتُ فِيهِ: جُمْلَةُ الصِّلَةِ، وَالضَّمِيرُ (ـهِ) عَائِدٌ
sections.notes: Because البَيْتُ is definite, الَّذِي is required, and ـهِ in فِيهِ acts as the returning pronoun ('in it').

sections.heading: Never Use الَّذِي After an Indefinite Noun
sections.body: Writing رَجُلٌ الَّذِي جَاءَ is ungrammatical in Arabic. For an indefinite noun ('a man who came'), omit the pronoun: رَجُلٌ جَاءَ.
